headline: Lost Fish Found: Indigenous Fisher Rediscovers Species Missing 40 Years
meta_description: Helen Asu caught a spinach pipefish near Papua New Guinea's Sepik River—a species unseen by science since 1985. Her knowledge proved invaluable.
summary_short: An Indigenous fisherwoman in Papua New Guinea caught a spinach pipefish, rediscovering a species lost to science for four decades and solving a scientific mystery.
body:
On the final day of a two-week expedition along Papua New Guinea's Sepik River, Indigenous fisherwoman Helen Asu made a discovery that stopped a team of researchers in their tracks. While fishing for prawns with a traditional hand net called an umben near Imbando village, she caught two small, greenish-brown fish that turned out to be spinach pipefish—a freshwater relative of seahorses unseen by science since 1985. The rediscovery of Microphis spinachioides, known only from the Sepik River, fills a gap of nearly four decades and answers the urgent question that had driven the expedition: does this rare species still exist? "It was honestly an incredible moment," said Jerrica Agebigo, the researcher who led the team, describing the instant she recognized the significance of what Asu had found.

The spinach pipefish is small—just 15 centimeters long—and uses its elongated snout to hunt tiny prey among water lilies and riverbank plants. So little is known about it that the original specimen used to describe the species was destroyed during World War II, and by 2016, it was classified as data deficient by the IUCN. It had become one of the 10 most sought-after species on the "Lost Fishes" list, among more than 300 freshwater fishes missing to science.

What makes this rediscovery particularly striking is how it happened. Agebigo's team—composed of local scientists and community members—had been traveling the Sepik, showing pictures to residents and asking fishers if they recognized the pipefish. The answer came not through scientific equipment or formal surveys, but through the daily work and deep ecological knowledge of a local fisher. "Without Helen's knowledge, experience and willingness to help us, we may not have found the species," Agebigo reflected. The moment underscores a vital truth: sometimes science's greatest breakthroughs depend on listening to those closest to the land.
